form.label: Advanced Workshop #1 — Infrastructure & Collector Health
form.description: The infrastructure capstone: host resource pressure, Kubernetes object state, and the OpenTelemetry Collector's own pipeline health — every panel built from the k8s_ws_metrics index with plain SPL.

div.p: The companion capstone to the Metrics & Traces dashboard. That one asks "how is my application behaving?" — this one asks the three questions you ask when the application is misbehaving and you need to know whether the platform underneath it is at fault: Is the host out of resources? Is Kubernetes actually running what I asked it to run? And is my telemetry pipeline still telling me the truth?

Everything below comes from a single index — k8s_ws_metrics — fed by three sources inside one Collector deployment: the hostmetrics receiver, the k8s_cluster receiver, and the Collector's own otelcol_* self-telemetry.

div.style: background:#FFF8E1; border-left:5px solid #F1813F; padding:10px 18px; border-radius:4px; margin-top:8px;
div.p: Fills in during Advanced Workshop #1. The workshop app installs every dashboard at once in Foundational Workshop #2, so this one is here early. Until you turn on the hostmetrics and k8s_cluster receivers, its panels are empty — that is expected, not a fault.

div.h3: Section 1 — Host Health: is the machine under the cluster running out of road?
div.p: Kubernetes will happily schedule pods onto a node that is already saturated; it schedules against requests, not against what is actually happening. These panels come from the hostmetrics receiver reading /proc directly, so they show the truth the scheduler cannot see.

panel.title: CPU Load Average (1m)
panel.description: Raw run-queue depth. Meaningless on its own until you divide it by core count — see the next panel.

search.query: | mstats avg(system.cpu.load_average.1m) as v WHERE index=k8s_ws_metrics span=1m | sort - _time | head 1 | eval value=round(v,2) | table value

panel.title: CPU Saturation (load ÷ cores)
panel.description: The number that actually matters. Under 100% the node keeps up with its work; sustained above 100% means processes are queueing for CPU and every latency number on the app dashboard will start to drift upward.

search.query: | mstats avg(system.cpu.load_average.1m) as l avg(system.cpu.logical.count) as c WHERE index=k8s_ws_metrics span=1m | sort - _time | head 1 | eval value=round(l/c*100,1) | table value

panel.title: Memory In Use
panel.description: Anonymous, non-reclaimable memory — the portion the kernel cannot hand back under pressure. This is what the OOM killer counts against you, not the cached figure.

search.query: | mstats avg(system.memory.usage) as v WHERE index=k8s_ws_metrics state=used span=1m | sort - _time | head 1 | eval value=round(v/1024/1024/1024,2) | table value

panel.title: Memory Utilization
panel.description: Used memory as a share of total physical RAM. Below ~70% you have room to schedule more pods; above ~90% the next deployment is a coin flip between eviction and an OOM kill.

search.query: | mstats avg(system.memory.usage) as v WHERE index=k8s_ws_metrics BY state | eventstats sum(v) as total | where state="used" | eval value=round(v/total*100,1) | table value

panel.title: Load Average Trend — 1m vs 5m vs 15m
panel.description: Read the ordering, not the values. 1m above 15m means load is climbing right now and you are watching a problem arrive; 1m below 15m means the spike has already passed and the cluster is recovering on its own. Three flat, overlapping lines is a node doing steady work — the only shape you want to see during a workshop run.

search.query: | mstats avg(system.cpu.load_average.1m) as "1-minute" avg(system.cpu.load_average.5m) as "5-minute" avg(system.cpu.load_average.15m) as "15-minute" WHERE index=k8s_ws_metrics span=$span_token$

panel.title: Memory Composition Over Time — Used vs Cached vs Free
panel.description: "Free memory is near zero" is almost never the problem — Linux deliberately spends idle RAM on page cache. The failure signature to look for is cached collapsing while used climbs: that is the kernel evicting its own cache to feed a growing process, and it is the last quiet moment before an OOM kill.

search.query: | mstats avg(system.memory.usage) WHERE index=k8s_ws_metrics AND (state=used OR state=cached OR state=free) span=$span_token$ BY state | xyseries _time state avg(system.memory.usage)

div.h3: Section 2 — Kubernetes Object State: is the cluster running what you declared?
div.p: Kubernetes is a declarative system, so almost every outage is a gap: desired minus available, requested minus scheduled, expected minus ready. The k8s_cluster receiver polls the API server for exactly those declared-vs-actual pairs, which is why this section is built out of differences rather than absolute numbers.

panel.title: Pod Phase by Namespace
panel.description: Every bar should be a single solid colour — one hundred percent Running. A second colour appearing in any namespace is the fastest visual signal in this dashboard: Pending means the scheduler could not place the pod (check Section 1 for the resource reason), Failed means it placed it and the container died.

search.query: | mstats latest(k8s.pod.phase) as phase WHERE index=k8s_ws_metrics BY k8s.namespace.name k8s.pod.name | eval Phase=case(phase=1,"Pending",phase=2,"Running",phase=3,"Succeeded",phase=4,"Failed",phase=5,"Unknown",true(),"Other") | rename "k8s.namespace.name" as Namespace | chart count over Namespace by Phase

panel.title: Container Restarts & Readiness
panel.description: A restart count above zero is the single most actionable signal Kubernetes emits — the container died and was resurrected, and nothing in the application logs will say so. Watch the count across refreshes: a static number is old scar tissue from cluster startup and can be ignored, but a number that increments while you watch is an active crash loop. A container that is restarting AND showing NOT READY is failing its probes right now and is currently serving no traffic.

search.query: | mstats latest(k8s.container.restarts) as restarts latest(k8s.container.ready) as ready WHERE index=k8s_ws_metrics BY k8s.namespace.name k8s.pod.name k8s.container.name | eval Ready=if(ready=1,"Ready","NOT READY") | eval Assessment=if(restarts>0,"Investigate — container has died before","Stable") | sort - restarts | rename "k8s.namespace.name" as Namespace, "k8s.pod.name" as Pod, "k8s.container.name" as Container, restarts as Restarts | table Namespace Pod Container Restarts Ready Assessment

panel.title: Workload Drift — Desired vs Available (Deployments & DaemonSets)
panel.description: The Gap column IS the outage. Kubernetes never reports "broken" — it reports that you asked for three replicas and two are available, and the missing one is the capacity your users are not getting. A DaemonSet gap is worse than it looks: because DaemonSets run one pod per node, a gap of one means an entire node has lost that capability — and if the missing pod is the Collector agent, you have gone blind on that node without a single error appearing anywhere else in this dashboard.

search.query: | mstats latest(k8s.deployment.desired) as desired latest(k8s.deployment.available) as available WHERE index=k8s_ws_metrics BY k8s.namespace.name k8s.deployment.name | eval Kind="Deployment" | rename "k8s.deployment.name" as Workload, "k8s.namespace.name" as Namespace | table Kind Namespace Workload desired available | append [ | mstats latest(k8s.daemonset.desired_scheduled_nodes) as desired latest(k8s.daemonset.ready_nodes) as available WHERE index=k8s_ws_metrics BY k8s.namespace.name k8s.daemonset.name | eval Kind="DaemonSet" | rename "k8s.daemonset.name" as Workload, "k8s.namespace.name" as Namespace | table Kind Namespace Workload desired available ] | eval Gap=desired-available | eval Status=if(Gap=0,"Healthy — declared state achieved","DEGRADED — capacity missing") | sort - Gap Kind Workload | rename desired as Desired, available as Available | table Kind Namespace Workload Desired Available Gap Status

panel.title: Scheduling Contract — CPU & Memory Requests vs Limits
panel.description: Requests are what the scheduler reserves; limits are what the kernel enforces. Every UNBOUNDED cell is a container that can consume the whole node — it will not be throttled, it will simply take CPU from its neighbours or push the node into an OOM kill that lands on some other pod. Conversely, a container whose request is far below its real usage will be packed onto a node that cannot actually feed it. Cross-reference this table with Section 1: if the node is saturated and an unbounded container is on it, you have found your culprit.

search.query: | mstats latest(k8s.container.cpu_request) as cr latest(k8s.container.cpu_limit) as cl latest(k8s.container.memory_request) as mr latest(k8s.container.memory_limit) as ml WHERE index=k8s_ws_metrics BY k8s.namespace.name k8s.container.name | eval "CPU Request"=if(isnull(cr),"none set",tostring(round(cr,3))." cores") | eval "CPU Limit"=if(isnull(cl),"UNBOUNDED",tostring(round(cl,3))." cores") | eval "Memory Request"=if(isnull(mr),"none set",tostring(round(mr/1024/1024,0))." MiB") | eval "Memory Limit"=if(isnull(ml),"UNBOUNDED",tostring(round(ml/1024/1024,0))." MiB") | eval Assessment=case(isnull(cl) AND isnull(ml),"Uncapped on both — can starve the whole node",isnull(cl) OR isnull(ml),"Partially uncapped — one resource unbounded",true(),"Fully capped — blast radius contained") | rename "k8s.namespace.name" as Namespace, "k8s.container.name" as Container | sort Namespace Container | table Namespace Container "CPU Request" "CPU Limit" "Memory Request" "Memory Limit" Assessment

panel.title: Pod Memory Usage vs. Declared Limit — Current State
panel.description: The Scheduling Contract panel above shows what each container declared; this shows what it is actually using, from the kubelet_stats receiver's real per-pod usage (dead until fixed live 2026-09-03 — see Advanced Workshop #1 §5's "kubelet_stats" section for the silent TLS failure that kept it at zero, and why this data lands in k8s_ws_petclinic_metrics rather than this dashboard's usual index). Confirmed live: five of six services sit between 43% and 55% of their declared memory limit; api-gateway is the outlier at 70.6% (1085 MiB working set against a 1536 MiB limit) — the same pod flagged as a "watch, not yet acted on" item after this morning's incident, now with a real number instead of a one-off snapshot. Working Set is the figure that matters for an OOM decision; Usage includes reclaimable cache and always reads a touch higher.

search.query: | mstats latest(k8s.pod.memory.usage) as usage_b latest(k8s.pod.memory.working_set) as ws_b WHERE index=k8s_ws_petclinic_metrics k8s.namespace.name=petclinic BY k8s.pod.name | rex field="k8s.pod.name" "^(?<Service>.+)-[a-z0-9]{8,10}-[a-z0-9]{5}$" | where isnotnull(Service) AND Service!="playwright-loadgen" | eval "Usage (MiB)"=round(usage_b/1024/1024,1), "Working Set (MiB)"=round(ws_b/1024/1024,1) | rename k8s.pod.name as Pod | table Service Pod "Usage (MiB)" "Working Set (MiB)" | join type=left Service [ | mstats latest(k8s.container.memory_limit) as ml WHERE index=k8s_ws_metrics k8s.namespace.name=petclinic BY k8s.container.name | rename k8s.container.name as Service | eval "Limit (MiB)"=round(ml/1024/1024,0) | table Service "Limit (MiB)" ] | eval "% of Limit"=round('Working Set (MiB)'/'Limit (MiB)'*100,1) | eval Assessment=case('% of Limit'>=90,"CRITICAL — approaching OOM kill",'% of Limit'>=70,"Watch — elevated but stable",true(),"Healthy headroom") | sort Service | table Service Pod "Working Set (MiB)" "Usage (MiB)" "Limit (MiB)" "% of Limit" Assessment

panel.title: Pod Memory Working Set Over Time by Service — Real Usage, kubelet_stats
panel.description: Same six services as the table above, this time as a trend rather than a single point — the exact signal that was missing this morning, when the only way to see per-pod memory over time was SSHing in and running docker stats by hand. Shared y-axis is deliberate here: the real range captured live was config-server at ~569 MiB up to api-gateway at ~1085 MiB, under a 2x spread, and every service shares a comparable 1280–1536 MiB declared limit — one shared scale lets you read all six services' real distance from that common ceiling at a glance. (Contrast the JVM Heap trellis on the Metrics & Traces dashboard, which deliberately uses an independent per-cell scale — there the point is preserving each JVM's own GC sawtooth shape, not comparing six services against one shared ceiling the way container memory limits let you do here.)

search.query: | mstats avg(k8s.pod.memory.working_set) as ws WHERE index=k8s_ws_petclinic_metrics k8s.namespace.name=petclinic span=$span_token$ BY k8s.pod.name | rex field="k8s.pod.name" "^(?<service>.+)-[a-z0-9]{8,10}-[a-z0-9]{5}$" | where isnotnull(service) AND service!="playwright-loadgen" | eval ws_mb=round(ws/1024/1024,2) | timechart span=$span_token$ avg(ws_mb) by service

div.h3: Section 3 — Collector Pipeline Health: the observability system observing itself
div.p: Every other panel in this workshop is only as trustworthy as the pipeline that delivered its data. A Collector that is silently dropping spans produces a dashboard that looks calmer during an incident, not noisier — which is the most dangerous failure mode an observability stack has. These panels read the Collector's own otelcol_* counters so you can prove the pipeline is intact before you trust anything above.

panel.title: Pipeline Throughput by Signal Type (items/sec exported)
panel.description: What the Collector is actually pushing downstream, per second, split by signal. Spans should track your load generator, metrics should be near-constant (scrape intervals do not care how busy you are), and logs should rise with error activity. The line to fear is any series dropping to zero and staying there while the others continue — that is one pipeline broken, not the Collector down, and it is invisible on every other panel in this workshop.

search.query: | mstats rate(otelcol_exporter_sent_spans) as "Spans/sec" rate(otelcol_exporter_sent_log_records) as "Log Records/sec" rate(otelcol_exporter_sent_metric_points) as "Metric Points/sec" WHERE index=k8s_ws_metrics span=$span_token$

panel.title: Data Loss Audit — Accepted vs Refused at the Receiver
panel.description: Any non-zero Refused figure is telemetry that was generated, sent, and then thrown away — those spans exist in your application's history but will never appear in any search you run. Zero across all three rows is the only acceptable state, and it is what lets you say "the gap in that chart is real" rather than "the gap in that chart might be us". If Refused starts climbing, look at the queue table below first: backpressure at the exporter is what makes a receiver start refusing.

search.query: | mstats latest(otelcol_receiver_accepted_spans) as acc latest(otelcol_receiver_refused_spans) as ref WHERE index=k8s_ws_metrics BY receiver | stats sum(acc) as Accepted sum(ref) as Refused | eval Signal="Traces (spans)" | append [ | mstats latest(otelcol_receiver_accepted_log_records) as acc latest(otelcol_receiver_refused_log_records) as ref WHERE index=k8s_ws_metrics BY receiver | stats sum(acc) as Accepted sum(ref) as Refused | eval Signal="Logs (records)" ] | append [ | mstats latest(otelcol_receiver_accepted_metric_points) as acc latest(otelcol_receiver_refused_metric_points) as ref WHERE index=k8s_ws_metrics BY receiver | stats sum(acc) as Accepted sum(ref) as Refused | eval Signal="Metrics (points)" ] | fillnull value=0 Accepted Refused | eval "Loss Rate %"=if((Accepted+Refused)>0, round(Refused/(Accepted+Refused)*100,4), 0) | eval Verdict=if(Refused=0,"No data loss — this signal is complete","DATA LOSS — telemetry discarded at ingest") | table Signal Accepted Refused "Loss Rate %" Verdict

panel.title: Exporter Queue Utilization — The Backpressure Early Warning
panel.description: Each exporter buffers in memory between the pipeline and the destination. Near-zero utilization means the backend is keeping up and the queue is draining as fast as it fills. A queue that is climbing is the earliest warning you get that a destination has slowed down — and it is a warning with a deadline, because when utilization hits 100% the Collector has nowhere left to put data and begins refusing it, which turns into non-zero Refused counts in the panel above. Rising numbers here give you minutes of lead time; the Data Loss Audit only tells you after the loss has already happened.

search.query: | mstats latest(otelcol_exporter_queue_size) as qsize latest(otelcol_exporter_queue_capacity) as qcap WHERE index=k8s_ws_metrics BY exporter otelcol.service.mode | eval "Utilization %"=round(qsize/qcap*100,2) | eval Headroom=qcap-qsize | eval Assessment=case(qsize/qcap>=0.8,"CRITICAL — refusals imminent",qsize/qcap>=0.3,"Backing up — destination is slowing",true(),"Draining normally") | sort - "Utilization %" exporter | rename exporter as Exporter, "otelcol.service.mode" as "Collector Role", qsize as "Queue Depth", qcap as "Queue Capacity", Headroom as "Slots Remaining" | table Exporter "Collector Role" "Queue Depth" "Queue Capacity" "Utilization %" "Slots Remaining" Assessment
